candidate.blueprint_locator: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control: apply infection-prevention principles, provide client education regarding infection-prevention measures, and recognize/report findings that increase risk of infection or injury from treatment devices.
candidate.blueprint_topic: Infection-prevention teaching for percutaneous orthopedic hardware
candidate.educational_objective: Teach clients with external fixation to follow their prescribed pin-site care protocol and promptly report findings suggestive of pin-site infection or hardware problems, recognizing that no single cleansing regimen is universally established for all patients.

options.A: I will follow the pin-site care instructions prescribed by my orthopedic team and report increasing redness, drainage, pain, swelling, fever, or a loose pin rather than inventing my own cleaning schedule or solution.
options.B: All external-fixator pin sites require the same cleansing solution and frequency, so I can use any standard internet protocol instead of the plan given by my care team.
options.C: Pin sites do not need ongoing assessment once I leave the hospital because infection occurs only during the initial placement procedure.
options.D: Drainage or increasing redness around a pin is expected and should be ignored unless the entire fixator becomes unstable.

candidate.rationale: A is correct. Current NCBI guidance emphasizes that pin-site care is important for external fixation, but available techniques vary and evidence does not support one universal cleansing protocol for every patient. Therefore, clients should follow the specific pin-site instructions provided by the orthopedic team rather than substitute an unapproved solution or schedule. Pin-site infection is a recognized complication, and ongoing assessment for erythema, drainage, pain, soft-tissue problems, or hardware loosening is important. B is incorrect because no single universal pin-care regimen has been established as superior. C is incorrect because pin-site infection and soft-tissue problems remain possible while the external fixator is in place and require ongoing monitoring. D is unsafe because new or increasing drainage or erythema can indicate pin-site infection and should prompt clinical review. The final item preserves infection-prevention teaching while removing the source's unsupported implication that one fixed cleaning frequency applies to all external fixators.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Current NCBI guidance directly supports individualized pin-site care rather than a universal cleansing protocol, ongoing monitoring for pin-site infection and soft-tissue problems, and reporting clinically concerning findings to the treating team.
candidate.source_locator: Section 'Pin Site Care': pin-site care is important to reduce infection risk, but techniques vary considerably and available data do not establish one universal superior protocol; drainage or erythema around pins warrants pin-site care/clinical attention. Section 'Complications': pin-site infection, osteomyelitis, pin/frame failure or loosening, soft-tissue and neurovascular complications. Section 'Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes': daily orthopedic/nursing assessment is essential for monitoring pin-site infection, soft-tissue integrity and neurovascular status, with issues reported to the treating clinician.
candidate.source_organization: National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI), StatPearls
